issues.legal_issue: A party’s admission in a signed and verified pleading from an earlier suit is admissible against that party in another suit, but is not conclusive.
material_facts: The defendants signed and verified a plaint in an earlier suit that stated that the joint-family member had died in 1939.
The plaintiff tendered that plaint in the later partition suit as evidence of the date of death.

The defendants argued that they had signed the earlier plaint without understanding its contents, but evidence showed that it was filed on their instructions and its contents had been read and understood by them.
The defendants did not establish that the admission was false or made under an error or misapprehension.
issues.conclusion: The statement in the earlier plaint was admissible under section 17 of the Indian Evidence Act as evidence against its makers in the later suit. It was strong evidence of the date of death, but was not conclusive and could have been shown to be untrue.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 makes no distinction between admissions in pleadings and other admissions. A statement in a plaint signed and verified by a party may be proved against that party in another suit, where it remains open to the party to show that it is untrue. The Court relied on D. S. Mohite v. S. I. Mohite and Marianski v. Cairns, and considered and explained the observations in Ramabai Shriniwas v. Bombay Government.

predicates.civil_proceeding_relying_on_prior_pleadi: The proceeding relies on a statement made in a pleading filed in an earlier suit.
predicates.party_signed_and_verified_prior_pleading: The party against whom the statement is used signed and verified the earlier pleading.
predicates.prior_pleading_contains_relevant_admissi: The earlier pleading contains an admission relevant to a matter in issue in the later proceeding.

issues.definition: When a civil proceeding relies on a relevant admission in an earlier pleading signed and verified by the party who made it, the admission is admissible but may still be shown to be untrue.

issues.legal_issue: A party may rely on a relevant admission in a pleading without accepting the pleading’s other statements, and the court may assess those statements separately.
material_facts: The plaintiff tendered the entire earlier plaint, which included both the statement about the date of death and statements alleging that the widow had surrendered her interest and was entitled only to maintenance.
The plaintiff relied on the statement about the date of death but disputed the allegations of surrender and maintenance.
The parties did not dispute that the widow had not surrendered her interest.
issues.conclusion: All statements in the plaint were admissible, but the court was not bound to accept all of them as correct; it could accept some statements and reject others.
issues.legal_principle: The admissibility of statements in a pleading does not require a party relying on one statement to accept the other statements, nor does it require the court to treat every statement as true. The Court applied section 17 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 and referred to D. S. Mohite v. S. I. Mohite and Ramabai Shriniwas v. Bombay Government.

rule.if: civil_proceeding_relying_on_prior_pleading and entire_prior_pleading_tendered and relevant_statement_relied_on and other_statements_disputed

predicates.civil_proceeding_relying_on_prior_pleadi: The proceeding relies on a pleading filed in an earlier suit.
predicates.entire_prior_pleading_tendered: The party relying on a statement tenders the entire earlier pleading as evidence.
predicates.relevant_statement_relied_on: The party relies on a statement in the pleading that is relevant to a matter in issue.
predicates.other_statements_disputed: The party disputes the correctness of other statements in the same pleading.

issues.definition: When a party tenders an entire earlier pleading, relies on a relevant statement, and disputes other statements in it, the court may assess and accept or reject those statements separately.

issues.legal_issue: A widow is entitled to the applicable share in joint-family property and may maintain a partition suit when the law granting that right applies to her husband’s death.
material_facts: The widow sought partition of joint-family property on the basis that her husband, a member of the joint family, died after the relevant property-right legislation took effect.

The Supreme Court found that the husband died in 1939, relying on the admission in the earlier plaint together with the widow’s and her witnesses’ evidence, and rejecting the defendants’ contrary evidence.
The husband held an eight-annas interest in the joint-family properties, and the property-right legislation applied to the agricultural land at issue.
It was conceded that, after the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 took effect, the widow held her share as full owner.
issues.conclusion: The widow was entitled to an eight-annas share in the joint-family estate and could maintain the partition suit. Following her death during the appeal, the purchaser could claim through her sale of the specified property.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the Hindu Women’s Rights to Property Act, 1937, read with the Bihar Hindu Women’s Rights to Property (Extension to Agricultural Land) Act, 1942, to the widow’s right to a share and to maintain partition. It also noted the concession that section 14 of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956 made her share her full property.

rule.if: partition_proceeding and widow_of_joint_family_member and husband_held_joint_family_property_interest and applicable_property_right_law_applied_to_property and husband_died_after_that_law_took_effect

predicates.partition_proceeding: The proceeding seeks partition of joint-family property.
predicates.widow_of_joint_family_member: The claimant is the widow of a member of the joint family whose property is to be partitioned.
predicates.husband_held_joint_family_property_inter: The husband held an interest in the joint-family property.
predicates.applicable_property_right_law_applied_to: A property-right law granting a widow an interest applies to the property in the proceeding.
predicates.husband_died_after_that_law_took_effect: The husband died after the applicable property-right law took effect.

issues.definition: When a widow seeks partition of property in which her joint-family-member husband held an interest, and the applicable law granting her a share applied when he died, she is entitled to that share and may maintain partition.

issues.legal_issue: An alienee of specific property from a co-owner may claim that property for allotment and separate possession in a general partition of the undivided property.
material_facts: The widow sold a specified parcel of land to the appellant while the property remained undivided.
The widow died while the partition appeal was pending, and the appellant continued the proceeding as her purchaser.
The parties conceded that, on a general partition, the appellant was entitled to allotment and separate possession of the land purchased.
issues.conclusion: The appellant was entitled, as an alienee of specific property from a co-owner, to allotment and separate possession of the purchased land on the general partition.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the purchaser as an alienee of specific property from a co-owner who could claim the rights of an alienee on a general partition of the undivided properties. The Court noted that all parties conceded the purchaser’s entitlement to allotment and separate possession.

predicates.general_partition_proceeding: The proceeding seeks a general partition of undivided property.
predicates.co_owner_sold_specific_undivided_propert: A co-owner sold a specific property that formed part of the undivided property.
predicates.purchaser_claims_under_that_sale: The purchaser seeks rights in the partition proceeding under the sale by the co-owner.

issues.definition: When a purchaser claims under a co-owner’s sale of specific undivided property in a general partition proceeding, the purchaser may receive allotment and separate possession of the purchased property.
